label: Stoicism
title: On the Shortness of Life – Seneca on Where Our Time Really Goes
thumbnail_text: Life is long if you use it
description: We complain that life is short. Almost two thousand years ago, Seneca argued the opposite: life is long enough – if you know how to use it. In this calm video essay we read his letter-essay On the Shortness of Life, written to a busy Roman official. We look at why we guard our money so carefully and give our time away so easily, what Seneca meant by the 'occupied', why waiting for tomorrow quietly costs us today, and a few simple ways to take your hours back.

sections.text:
If someone tried to take fifty euros out of your wallet, you would stop them immediately. You would be angry for the rest of the day.

But if someone took an hour of your afternoon with something that did not matter to you, an unnecessary meeting, a pointless argument, a scroll that never seemed to end, you would probably not even notice.

We guard our money like a treasure. And we hand out our time as if we had an endless supply.

Almost two thousand years ago, a Roman philosopher noticed exactly this. And he wrote a short essay about it that people are still reading today.

sections.heading: A Letter to a Busy Man
sections.text:
Lucius Annaeus Seneca was one of the most famous writers of ancient Rome. He was a Stoic philosopher, a playwright, a very wealthy man, and for some years an adviser to the emperor Nero. So he knew a great deal about power, ambition, and busy days.

The essay we now call On the Shortness of Life is addressed to a man named Paulinus. Paulinus held an important post. He was responsible for Rome's grain supply, which meant that a whole city depended on his work.

The essay was probably written in the middle of the first century. Its exact date is debated. But its message is clear, and in places surprisingly personal. Seneca is not writing to a lazy man. He is writing to a capable, responsible, overworked one. Someone, perhaps, a little like many of us.

sections.heading: Life Is Long Enough

quote.lead: Seneca begins with a complaint he heard everywhere. Life is too short. We barely begin to live, and it is already over. His reply, in our own rendering of the Latin, is one short sentence:
quote.text: Life is long, if you know how to use it.
quote.author: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2.1

sections.text:
For Seneca, the problem is not the amount of time we are given. It is what we do with it. A large fortune can be lost in a few years by someone careless, he says, while a small one can grow in the hands of someone who manages it well. Time works the same way.

We do not receive a short life. We make it short.

And then he begins to look, very closely, at where the time actually goes. Some people spend their years in endless ambition, always reaching for the next position. Some spend them in the service of others who will never thank them. Some drift from one plan to the next without finishing anything. Some spend it all in pleasures that leave them empty.

None of these people, Seneca says, are really living. They are merely passing time.

sections.heading: Guarding Money, Wasting Time

quote.lead: Then comes the observation that makes this essay feel so modern. In our rendering:
quote.text: Nobody can be found who is willing to share out his money; but among how many people does each of us divide up his life!
quote.author: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3.1

sections.text:
People defend their property, Seneca notes. If there is a dispute about land, they rush to court. But they let others walk into their lives freely. They allow every visitor, every request, every obligation to take a piece of their time.

Why? Because time is invisible. We cannot see it leaving. Money sits in a drawer, but hours slip past without a sound.

Seneca suggests a small exercise. Look back over your life, and try to count how much of it was truly yours. How much went to quarrels, to worries, to people who wanted something from you, to waiting. Many people, he says, would be shocked by how little remains.

And there is a strange contradiction in all of this. He puts it like this: we fear everything as if we were mortal, and desire everything as if we were immortal.

sections.heading: The Occupied
sections.text:
Seneca has a special word for people who have lost their lives to busyness. In Latin they are the occupati. The occupied.

They are not necessarily people with a lot of work. They are people whose minds are always somewhere else. Full of plans, demands and distractions, they never have time to be present for their own lives.

Seneca is sharp about this. Nothing, he says, is less the business of a busy person than living. And living, he adds, is the hardest thing to learn. It takes a whole lifetime.

The occupied often promise themselves that they will really start living later. After this project. After this promotion. Once they retire. Seneca asks a simple, uncomfortable question. Who guaranteed you that later? And is it not a little strange to save only the leftovers of life for yourself?

Today, our occupations might look different. Notifications, inboxes, endless small tasks. But the feeling Seneca describes is familiar. Days that are completely full, and somehow empty at the same time.

sections.heading: Waiting for Tomorrow

quote.lead: There is one sentence in the essay that goes right to the centre of the problem. In our rendering:
quote.text: The greatest obstacle to living is expectation, which hangs upon tomorrow and loses today.
quote.author: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 9.1

sections.text:
We tend to treat the present as a waiting room. A place we have to get through, on the way to something better. The weekend, the holiday, the next stage of life.

But the present is the only part of time we actually hold. The past is gone, and the future is uncertain. To give up today for a tomorrow that may look completely different is, in Seneca's eyes, a very poor trade.

It can help to do a little arithmetic. A life of eighty years is a little over four thousand weeks. That is not a frightening number. But it is a finite one. And each of those weeks is made of ordinary days, most of which will look very much like today.

This does not mean that we should never plan. Seneca himself made plenty of plans. It means that planning should serve the life we are living, not replace it.

sections.heading: Taking Your Hours Back
sections.text:
So what can we actually do? Seneca's own answer was that the people who truly live are those who make time for wisdom, for reading, for thinking about what matters. Only they, he says, are really at leisure. But we can translate his advice into a few small steps.

First, notice where your time goes. For one ordinary day, simply observe it, the way you might look at a bank statement. Not to judge yourself. Just to see.

Second, guard one part of each day. Even half an hour that belongs to you, protected like money you would never hand to a stranger. Use it for something you value, a book, a walk, a real conversation.

Third, stop postponing the things you care about to an imagined later. If there is someone you want to call, a project you want to begin, a place you want to see, ask yourself what small step you could take this week.

Seneca did not believe life was short. He believed it was long enough, if we stop giving it away without noticing.

The hours are passing either way. The only question is whether we will be there for them.

short.hook: Seneca's answer to 'life is too short'
short.title: Life is long, if you know how to use it
short.text:
If someone took fifty euros from your wallet, you would stop them. If someone took an hour of your afternoon, you would probably not even notice.

Seneca saw this two thousand years ago. Nobody wants to share out their money, he wrote. But we divide our lives among so many people.

He called the endlessly busy the occupied. Always planning to live later. After this project. After this promotion.

His answer was simple. Life is long, if you know how to use it.

So guard one part of each day. The hours are passing either way.
